         Staff of the Utility Division ("Staff") of the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

(the “Commission”) hereby files Staff’s Post-Hearing Brief pursuant to the deadlines set by the

Hearing Examiners’ Order on Post Hearing Briefs (“Briefing Order”), issued on July 28, 2026.

Because it relies on an unreasonable and unsupported revenue requirement, and jurisdictional

and class allocation outcomes, the stipulation reached by the signatories in this docket is not

in the public interest. Staff urges the Commission to reject the stipulation and ensure fair, just,

and reasonable rates for all of SPS’s ratepayers.

                    I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

      This case concerns the Commission’s obligation to reconcile its policy favoring stipulated

resolution of contested issues with its statutory duty to ensure that every rate is fair, just, and

reasonable and in the public interest. That obligation is particularly important here because of the

substantial disparity between SPS’s initial revenue request and the $90 million base-rate increase

to which the Signatories have agreed. As the table below shows, SPS’s prior rate cases have

routinely resulted in significant authorized increases and ROEs after substantial reductions from

the Company’s opening positions. The fact of a reduction from an initial request, however, does

not itself establish that the resulting rates are lawful or reasonable; rather, the Commission must

determine whether the stipulated outcome is affirmatively supported by the evidence and

independently satisfies the governing statutory standard. 1

          Staff agrees that the Commission must evaluate a comprehensive stipulation as an integrated

package negotiated by its signatories. But that principle creates no presumption of approval. Under

1.2.2.20(B) NMAC and NMSA 1978, Sections 62-8-1 and 62-8-7, the Commission must determine

argument. The Stipulation fails that test. It authorizes a $90 million base-rate increase—

approximately $42.3 million more than Staff’s $47.691 million supported revenue deficiency—

while preserving unsupported and inequitable jurisdictional- and class-allocation outcomes that

affect both the amount charged to New Mexico customers and the customers who bear those

charges.

              The weight of the record evidence, therefore, does not support approval of the

Stipulation as filed. To protect the public interest, the Commission should either reject the

Stipulation, as a whole, and decide the disputed issues on the fully developed evidentiary

record, or permit the Signatories to consider the alternative reflected in Staff Exhibit A,

increase in total revenues.

        2.      SPS’s Application is based on a future test year using a Base Period of July 1, 2024,

            Critical background to this question is that at the time of the Final Order in Docket No.

17-00044-UT, no transfer market existed for SPS to sell the PTCs and that the Final Order in that

case allowed SPS to create a deferred tax asset (DTA) with a carrying cost and placed a time cap

methodology so the DTA does not carry forward for an unreasonable amount of time. Staff

believes it is in the public interest to limit the amount of time SPS may carry forward a DTA as a

condition of approval of any stipulation in this matter. This view is consistent with the Direct

Testimony of Peterson Brossy which stated that it was in the public interest to not provide any

incentive to hold a DTA balance when he recommend the Commission limit the return on the DTA

to the company’s weighted cost of debt, because if SPS was granted a high return that could be an

incentive to accrue PTCs in a DTA without transferring them or using them to reduce the

company’s federal tax liability. Staff concludes that it is in the public interest to have a time limit

on SPS’s PTC DTA. Staff concludes a time cap on the accrual of a DTA is an added layer of

customer protection. In addition, changes in the PTC laws may cause changes to transferability.

Taxpayers may receive a Production Tax Credit for ten years, beginning when the underlying

facility is placed in service. 3 In Case No. 17-00044-UT, the Commission put a time limit of the

end of 2025 (about 8 years) on the DTA from wind facility PTCs. 4 Therefore, in response to the

Hearing Examiner’s question, Staff recommends a time cap of 10 years to ensure that PTCs

accrued in a DTA do not carry forward for an unreasonable amount of time.

 IV. SPS HAS NOT PROVEN THAT ITS FUTURE TEST YEAR REFLECTS
   CONDITIONS WHEN RATES WILL BE IN EFFECT

         A. SPS Bears the Burden to Prove a Verifiable Future Test Year

         Under NMSA 1978, Section 62-6-14(D), the Commission must set rates based on the test

period that it determines “best reflects the conditions to be experienced during the period when the

rates determined by the commission take effect.” A future test period is therefore not a license to

use unverified or stale projections; it is a statutory mechanism for establishing rates that reflect

conditions expected during the period of rate effectiveness. NMSA 1978, §§ 62-3-3(P), 62-6-

14(D).

         SPS retains the burden to prove that the rate increase it seeks is just and reasonable. NMSA

1978, § 62-8-7(A). In an FTY case, that burden includes proving that material forecasted expenses,

rate-base additions, revenues, load, allocators, and other cost-of-service inputs are sufficiently

supported to represent expected conditions when new rates will be in effect. NMSA 1978, §§ 62-

6-14(D), 62-8-7(A). SPS has failed to prove that its forecasts represent the conditions when the

new rates will take effect, as detailed below, and for this reason alone, does not comport with

Section 62-16-4 (D) and should be rejected.

         The Future Test Year Rule requires that material changes between the historic base period

and future test period be separately identified, explained, justified, and linked to the historic base

period and linkage data. 17.1.3.17(A) NMAC. “Linkage data” is a specific and detailed description

of all line items between the end of the base period and the beginning of the future test period, and

its purpose is to create a verifiable link between historical base-period data and future-test-period

data. (emphasis added). 17.1.3.7(H) NMAC. The Rule further requires that projections be

retraceable to historical data or be supported by a fully understandable new basis; assumptions,

escalation factors, contingency provisions, and changes in activity levels must be quantified and

           B. SPS’s Own Post-Filing Revisions Confirm That Its Original Future Test Year Did
           Not Reliably Reflect Expected Conditions

           SPS originally requested a New Mexico retail FTY revenue deficiency of $175.355 million.

After filing, SPS filed a Comprehensive List of Revisions reducing the FTY revenue deficiency

by $3.054 million. 8 SPS then filed a correction to its FTY depreciation expense that reduced total-

company depreciation expense by $11.833 million and reduced the New Mexico retail FTY

revenue requirement by $4.749 million. Id. Following those post-filing revisions, SPS’s requested

New Mexico retail base-rate increase was approximately $167.551 million.

           SPS’s own post-filing revisions demonstrate that its original FTY filing did not reliably

represent the conditions expected during the rate-effective period. NMSA 1978, § 62-6-14(D).

Once later information demonstrates that a material forecasted cost is incorrect, the Commission

should use the corrected and verifiable value, rather than retain an earlier FTY forecast merely

because it appeared in the original application. 17.1.3.17(A), (C)–(D) NMAC. The depreciation

correction also confirms the need for the Commission to examine whether other significant FTY

to keep those numbers current. 11 When asked whether the shortfall figure had changed, he

reasonable, or whether the FTY revenue requirement was updated to reflect SPS’s changing

        SPS's Comprehensive Stipulation, is a non-unanimous, contested stipulation. The

Commission's procedural rule governing stipulations draws a sharp distinction between

uncontested and contested stipulations, and that distinction controls the standard of review here.

Where “some, but not all, of the parties to a proceeding, including staff, enter into a stipulation,”

the stipulation is a "contested stipulation" under 1.2.2.20(B) NMAC, and “[t]he proponents of the

stipulation have the burden of supporting the stipulation with sufficient evidence and legal

argument to allow the commission to approve it.” 90. The rule does not shift any burden to Staff or

other opposing parties to disprove the Stipulation, nor does it afford the Stipulation, as a package,

any presumption of reasonableness merely because it resolves “some or all of the issues” as

between the signing parties. 91

        A settlement stipulation is binding only if approved by the Commission 92 NMAC.

Commission precedent applies that approval standard through four criteria, asking whether (1) the

stipulation resulted from serious bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties; (2) the

stipulation, as a whole, benefits customers and the public interest; (3) the stipulation, as a whole,

proof that the rates are fair, just and reasonable and in the public interest, as a whole. It is

significant that the only party that represents the public interest, which is Staff, opposes the

Stipulation. The relevant question for the Commission is whether the resulting rates are supported

by the record and reflect conditions that can be reliably expected to exist when those rates take

effect. As discussed above, substantial reductions from a utility’s opening position can still leave
